attribution.note: Marcus's own words, repeating what he told a journalist and endorsing it in his own post.

semantics.note: Accurately restates a claim about what Shumer's essay contains. The scope (latest coding systems, whole complex apps, without errors) is kept.

contract.note: Reading 'actual data' as systematic measurement rather than anecdote is the ordinary reading. Treating the METR citation as data only if it bears on error-free apps is fair. Shumer's 'usually perfect' versus 'without errors' is flagged, but 'no corrections needed' supports the reading.

evidence.note: Shumer's essay text (labelled secondary_summary, but it is the primary essay). The 'no corrections needed' claim rests only on his own experience.
The whole-app example is a personal anecdote ('my Monday'), with no error rates or test data.
Says code 'works correctly' at scale, with no source or data cited.
The METR citation is data, but on task length at 50% success, not on error-free building of whole apps.

reviews.rationale: The essay's claims that whole apps come out correctly with no corrections rest on Shumer's own experience. The only data cited (METR task length) does not measure error-free building of complete apps. Marcus's description of the essay holds.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence, citing TechCrunch as an illustration.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'some coders' qualifier and the claim that coders report this. It is about reports, not a population rate.

contract.note: Reading this as documented reports in the cited story is fair. 'Some coders' sets a low bar, and the comparison of gains with burnout is qualitative.

evidence.note: The Loizos TechCrunch story exists (2026-02-09). It quotes an engineer working the same amount or more with AI.
A Hacker News commenter quoted in the story says stress has tripled while productivity rose only about 10%. This directly matches 'modest gains relative to burnout'.
The Berkeley/HBR research reports burnout among AI adopters. Its point that the augmentation is real tempers, but does not negate, the 'some coders' claim.
A later METR page on AI coding speed. It bears only on the uncontroversial 'wicked fast' framing.

reviews.rationale: The cited TechCrunch story exists and documents an engineer reporting more work, plus a tech worker reporting tripled stress against about 10% productivity gains. That meets the low bar set by 'some coders'. The research finding that augmentation is real does not undercut the reports.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words, agreeing with part of what Shumer said.

semantics.note: Faithful paraphrase: recent systems can be left to run more autonomously than before.

contract.note: Reading 'let things rip more' as longer autonomous tasks with less human help is the ordinary reading. The METR yardstick is reasonable, and the flat 80% horizon is flagged.

evidence.note: METR (via a faithful LessWrong reproduction, December 2025): Opus 4.5's 50% horizon of about 4h49m was the highest published to date.
Anthropic's own announcement (2026-02-05) that Opus 4.6 sustains agentic tasks for longer. A company disclosure, consistent with METR.
The 80% horizon stayed flat at 27–32 minutes. Gains were at moderate reliability, which fits Marcus's 'sometimes' caveat.

reviews.rationale: METR measured a record 50% time horizon for a late-2025 model, and the developer reports longer agentic runs. The flat 80% horizon limits how far the gain goes, but does not contradict 'can let things rip more'. Marcus himself framed the gain as sometimes working.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words, repeating what he told a journalist and endorsing it in his post.

semantics.note: The core reliability claim is kept, including 'every', 'or even close' and five hours. The clause that Shumer's blog ignores errors is dropped, and the presupposition that errors are common is restated as its own claim. That is a minor and acceptable change.

contract.note: Using METR's 80% horizon as the reliability yardstick is fair, and even generous to AI, since 'without error' implies a higher bar. Treating the vague hallucination clause as secondary is reasonable.

evidence.note: METR via LessWrong: Opus 4.5's 80% horizon was 27 minutes, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max's 32 minutes. Both are far below five hours.
METR's tasks are mainly software, ML and cybersecurity, not every human task. The page is dated after the claim period.
Wikipedia, May 2026: the best 80% horizon was still about 3 hours. This is after the claim period, so context only.

reviews.rationale: Around the post date, frontier 80% time horizons were about 27–32 minutes, even on software-focused tasks. That is nowhere near reliable five-hour performance across all tasks. The unquantified clause about errors being common in everyday use is unverified but not contradicted, and the contract treats it as secondary.
